author: Roberts
text: It [the study] is based on the major hypothesis that every small group, like groups of other sizes, defines an independent and unique culture . . . the description of any culture is a statement of ordered habit relationships. . . . The data in the field were collected on the theory that the culture of a group could be defined in terms of its shared habits. On analysis, it was found that, although important because it implies common learning, understanding, and action, the shared habit relationship was not the only one which was significant.
note: K&K Part II, Group D-III (Emphasis on Habit), page footnote 14 — the fourth D-III entry, after the three numbered statements. Printed p. 60 (PDF 63), read by the assistant at 300 dpi. The text column holds the two quoted Roberts passages. The footnote frames them as: Roberts, a pupil of Murdock, says (1951, pp. 3, 6), and closes with K&K's own comment that Roberts also (p. 3) speaks of a habit as "a way of behaving," linking to the C-I group. The footnote marker 14 is the page-footnote number, not a statement number.
